1:
How the psalmist came to be at the end of the earth is the standing question. Adam Clarke says the word should be translated land rather than earth, takes it of the country beyond the Euphrates, and dates the psalm to the close of the captivity. John Calvin puts it in Absalom’s conspiracy, arguing that had David not been an exile he could not have spoken so; the phrase means the place of his banishment, cut off from the temple and the royal city. Matthew Henry reads it as the remotest and obscurest corner of the country. Charles Ellicott will not let it settle anything: it is a hyperbole for a great distance, used by Isaiah of Assyria at Isaiah 5:26, natural in an exile’s mouth but not to be pressed to support any theory of the date. Keil and Delitzsch defend the Davidic title against those who push the psalm down to the exile or later, and dismiss the proposal that the king spoken of is Cyrus as another worthless bubble.

Matthew Henry draws the practical inference. Wherever we are we may find a way open to the throne of grace, since heaven is equally accessible from all places; and what separates us from our other comforts should drive us the nearer to God. He applies the same logic to the overwhelmed heart: it is not so far sunk that it cannot be lifted up in prayer, and because it is ready to be overwhelmed, therefore he will cry, since by that means it will be supported. C.H. Spurgeon presses the difference between praying and being heard. The psalmist is not content to give his sorrows vent but wants actual audience of heaven; Pharisees may rest in their prayers, but living children of God never rest till their supplications have entered the ears of the Lord. Whatever else fails to move him, praying breath is never spent in vain.

John Gill makes the distance a comfort: the people of God are sometimes forced to flee far off, and have a God still to go to, who is a God afar off as well as at hand. Charles Ellicott attends to the words for the overwhelming: literally in the covering of my heart, the verb used of valleys covered with corn and metaphorically of the garment of heaviness that wraps a sad heart — Tennyson’s muffled round with woe.

The rock is read at three heights. Charles Ellicott renders the clause literally, upon the rock lead me, and takes it as compressed for lead me to the rock too high for me to climb by myself, and place me there; the elevated rock is a symbol of security not obtainable without divine help. John Wesley asks only to be conveyed into some secure fortress. Adam Clarke allows three senses: a place of refuge, a metaphor Calmet interprets of the liberty granted the Jews by Cyrus, and the reading of the fathers, who think Christ is meant by this high rock. He adds that the Jews were always more pious in their afflictions than in their own land at ease — for who can bear prosperity?

Augustine of Hippo denies that a single man is speaking at all. The voice of the psalm we ought to acknowledge as our own — not of those now present merely, but of us throughout the whole world, from the East even to the West. He speaks here as if one man, but he is not one man; it is the Unity that is speaking, and in Christ we are all one man, of whom the Head is in heaven and the members are yet toiling on earth. What one man, he asks, cries from the ends of the earth? None but that inheritance of which it was said to the Son, demand of me and I will give thee the nations.
3:
The two figures of the third verse are given briefly. John Gill makes the shelter a refuge from avenging justice, a hiding place from the storms of divine wrath and a screen from Satan’s fiery darts. Adam Clarke keeps to his captivity setting: through the whole duration of it God marvellously dealt with the poor Jews, so that although they were cast down they were not utterly forsaken. Charles Ellicott adds only a cross-reference for the strong tower, to Proverbs 18:10.

What tabernacle is meant is the question of the next verse, and Charles Ellicott leaves it open. It is difficult to decide whether the word indicates the Mosaic tabernacle, and so indexes the poem’s date, or whether the tent is a general figure for the protection of God; it certainly recalls Psalm 23:6. John Gill offers three senses without choosing: the protection of the Lord, as in a shepherd’s tent; or the tabernacle of the congregation, the house of God; or the tabernacle prefigured by that one below, where he knew he should dwell to all eternity. Kimchi, he adds, understands for ever as a long time, while Jarchi explains it of both this world and the world to come.

The mood of the verbs divides two of them. Charles Ellicott would make both petitions rather than promises: let me be a guest in thy tent, and let me find refuge under the shelter of thy wings. John Wesley takes them as confident expectation instead — I shall, I doubt not, be restored to the tabernacle and worship thee there all my days.

Adam Clarke supplies an authorship note and then a judgement of taste. He reports Calmet’s observation that most psalms composed during and after the captivity had Levites and priests for their authors, which accounts for the ardent desire so often expressed of seeing the temple and spending their lives there in their sacred office. He then paraphrases the verse in its own terms — there I shall sojourn, be at rest, be covered with thy wings, as a bird in its nest is covered with the wings of its mother — and defends the manner of it: such simple comparisons, drawn from rural affairs and ordinary occurrences, are more consolatory in circumstances like these than allegories derived from the most sublime subjects.
5:
The vows are treated first, and treated as a debt God graciously honours. Matthew Henry distinguishes two things heard: the vows themselves, which God accepted and remembered, as he put Jacob in mind of his at Genesis 31:13; and the prayers that went with them, which he answered. God is a witness to all our vows, Henry says, and keeps an account of them — for he that hears the vows we made will make us hear respecting them if they are not made good. C.H. Spurgeon allows that vows may rightly be joined with prayers when lawful and truly for God’s glory, but marvels that God takes any notice of the vows of such faithless creatures as we are: what we promise him is his due already, and yet he accepts our vows as if we were not his servants but free suitors who might give or withhold at pleasure. John Gill notes that vows are so called because it was usual to make them in trouble, and that Kimchi and Ben Melech take the past tense here for the future, given the certainty of the prayers being heard.

What the heritage is they answer in three ways. Charles Ellicott observes that as the received version runs the heritage is length of days, promised generally to those who fear the Lord and particularly to Israel and its kings, and that Deuteronomy 17:19 may have been in the psalmist’s mind; but the Greek and Latin read to them that fear thy name, and then the heritage is Canaan. John Wesley and Adam Clarke take it of access rather than land — the singular mercy of living in God’s land, enjoying his presence and worshipping in his tabernacle, the privilege of enjoying him in his ordinances, which is the heritage all who fear him prize above everything. Matthew Henry makes it the possession of a peculiar people: there is a people in the world that fear God’s name, and a heritage peculiar to them, present comforts that are earnests of future bliss. C.H. Spurgeon presses the sharing: we are joint-heirs with all the saints, so that if we suffer or are in poverty, all this is contained in the title-deeds of the heritage of the chosen. Those we are to sup with, he says, we may well be content to dine with.

The king of the sixth verse divides them sharply. Adam Clarke denies that any earthly monarch can be meant. The words are very emphatic and can refer to no ordinary person — literally, days upon days thou wilt add to the king, and his years shall be like the generations of this world and of the world to come — a paraphrase he had made, he notes, before consulting the Chaldee. It is Christ as Mediator who shall abide before God for ever, and neither to David nor to any earthly sovereign can these words be applied.

John Gill allows both. It may mean David himself, whose life was in danger through his son’s conspiracy and who was yet assured that he should live many years, especially in his posterity; or rather, as the Targum has it, the King Messiah, and Kimchi observes that if the psalm respects the captivity the King is the Messiah. Understood so, it speaks of Christ’s life as man, who though he died lives for evermore, of the continuance of his spiritual seed, and of the duration of his kingdom, which shall have no end. John Wesley takes the middle position, referring the words to the years of David’s life and reign, but adding that he speaks so because his kingdom was not like Saul’s but established to him and his heirs, and because Christ his heir should in his own person possess the kingdom for ever. Charles Ellicott makes only a formal point, that the verse should be read as a prayer.
7:
Who abides before God for ever divides the seventh verse. John Gill reads it of Christ, who being raised from the dead was received up into the presence of God and sat down at his right hand, where he abides for ever, a Priest upon his throne with an unchangeable priesthood. Adam Clarke agrees and fills it out: he shall ever appear in the presence of God for us, and sits at the right hand of the Majesty on high, having undertaken that office after making atonement for our sins by his sacrificial offering; as Mediator his attendants will always be mercy and truth, since he dispenses the mercy of God and so fulfils the truth of the various promises and predictions that preceded his incarnation. John Wesley keeps the verse with David instead — abiding in the throne, living and ruling as in God’s presence, serving God and worshipping him in his tabernacle — and takes the pair as truth in giving the mercies promised and mercy in giving such further blessings as he needs. Charles Ellicott would render the clause may he sit enthroned.

The second half of the verse is the harder half, and Adam Clarke gathers five renderings of the one obscure particle behind it. Some translate it who or what; others make it number thou, from a verb meaning to count; Houbigant, followed by Bishop Lowth, would emend it and read mercy and truth from Jehovah shall preserve him; the Anglo-Saxon gives mildheartedness and soothfastness his, who seeketh, which is nearly the rendering of the Old Psalter, mercy and soothfastness of him, who shall seek; and Dr Kennicott holds the word a Syriasm to be translated as an entreaty, I beseech thee, O that — on which ground Coverdale rendered it, O let thy loving mercy and faithfulness preserve him. Clarke takes that last sense to be the true one. Charles Ellicott works the same difficulty more briefly, preferring appoint to prepare, noting that the Greek had a different reading, and reporting an ingenious emendation suggested by comparison with another psalm, which would give let mercy and truth continually preserve him.

The closing verse is read as the answer to all that went before. John Gill lists what the praise is for: the hearing of his prayers, the goodly heritage given him, the prolonging of the King’s life, and the preparing of mercy and truth to preserve him; and the singing is to be constant, not in this world only but in that to come. Adam Clarke reads the daily performance of the vows in the Hebrew idiom, day by day, each day as it succeeds, acting according to what he had often purposed and as often promised. He then gives the Chaldee, which he calls remarkable: thus I will praise thy name for ever, when I shall perform my vows in the day of the redemption of Israel, and in the day in which the King Messiah shall be anointed, that he may reign. And he ends the chapter with an observation of his own — that the ancient Jews were full of the expectation of the Messiah, while the Jews of the present day have given up their hope.
